entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12716"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> Micah was a native of Moresheth, not the same as Mareshah in <reference osisRef="Mic.1.15">Mi 1:15</reference>, but the town called Moresheth-gath (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.14">Mi 1:14</reference>), which lay near Eleutheropolis, west of Jerusalem, on the border of the Philistine country; so called to distinguish it from Moresheth of Judah. His full name is Micaiah (not the Micaiah mentioned <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">1Ki 22:8</reference>, the son of Imlah), signifying, Who is like Jehovah? The time of his prophesying is stated in the introduction to be in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, that is, between 757 and 699 B.C. Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jr 26:18</reference>) quotes <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>, as delivered in the reign of Hezekiah. He was thus a contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea. The idolatries practised in the reign of Ahaz accord with Micah's denunciations of such gross evils, and confirm the truth of the time assigned <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>. His prophecies are partly against Israel (Samaria), partly against Judah. As Samaria, Israel's metropolis, was taken first, and Jerusalem, the capital of Judah subsequently, in the introductory heading, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>, Samaria is put first, then Jerusalem. He prophesies the capture of both; the Jews' captivity and restoration; and the coming and reign of Messiah. His style is full, round, and perspicuous; his diction pure, and his parallelisms regular. His description of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">19</reference>) is not surpassed by any elsewhere in Scripture. The similarity between Isaiah and Micah in some passages (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.3">Mi 4:1-3</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>) is to be accounted for by their being contemporaries, acquainted with each other's inspired writings, and having the same subjects for their theme. Hengstenberg maintains that the passage in Micah is the original. Isaiah was somewhat the older, being a prophet in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham's predecessor, whereas Micah began his prophecies under Jotham.<div eID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23521" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> The book consists of two parts: (1) the first through fifth chapters; (2) the sixth and seventh chapters, a dialogue or contestation between Jehovah and His people, in which He reproaches them with their unnatural and ungrateful conduct, and threatens judgment for their corruptions, but consoles them with the promise of restoration from captivity.<div eID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> Micah stands sixth of the minor prophets in the Hebrew canon, but third in the Septuagint.<div eID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.1.1-Mic.1.16">Mi 1:1-16</reference>. God's Wrath against Samaria and Judah; the Former Is to Be Overthrown; Such Judgments in Prospect Call for Mourning.</title> <div sID="gen23525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12716"/>[]
entries.content_plain: INTRODUCTION Micah was a native of Moresheth, not the same as Mareshah in Mi 1:15 , but the town called Moresheth-gath ( Mi 1:14 ), which lay near Eleutheropolis, west of Jerusalem, on the border of the Philistine country; so called to distinguish it from Moresheth of Judah. His full name is Micaiah (not the Micaiah mentioned 1Ki 22:8 , the son of Imlah), signifying, Who is like Jehovah? The time of his prophesying is stated in the introduction to be in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, that is, between 757 and 699 B.C. Jeremiah ( Jr 26:18 ) quotes Mi 3:12 , as delivered in the reign of Hezekiah. He was thus a contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea. The idolatries practised in the reign of Ahaz accord with Micah's denunciations of such gross evils, and confirm the truth of the time assigned Mi 1:1 . His prophecies are partly against Israel (Samaria), partly against Judah. As Samaria, Israel's metropolis, was taken first, and Jerusalem, the capital of Judah subsequently, in the introductory heading, Mi 1:1 , Samaria is put first, then Jerusalem. He prophesies the capture of both; the Jews' captivity and restoration; and the coming and reign of Messiah. His style is full, round, and perspicuous; his diction pure, and his parallelisms regular. His description of Jehovah ( Mi 7:18 , 19 ) is not surpassed by any elsewhere in Scripture. The similarity between Isaiah and Micah in some passages (compare Mi 4:1-3 , with Is 2:2-4 ) is to be accounted for by their being contemporaries, acquainted with each other's inspired writings, and having the same subjects for their theme. Hengstenberg maintains that the passage in Micah is the original. Isaiah was somewhat the older, being a prophet in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham's predecessor, whereas Micah began his prophecies under Jotham. The book consists of two parts: (1) the first through fifth chapters; (2) the sixth and seventh chapters, a dialogue or contestation between Jehovah and His people, in which He reproaches them with their unnatural and ungrateful conduct, and threatens judgment for their corruptions, but consoles them with the promise of restoration from captivity. Micah stands sixth of the minor prophets in the Hebrew canon, but third in the Septuagint. CHAPTER 1 Mi 1:1-16 . God's Wrath against Samaria and Judah; the Former Is to Be Overthrown; Such Judgments in Prospect Call for Mourning. []

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">2. all that therein is--</hi>Hebrew, "whatever fills it." Micaiah, son of Imlah, our prophet's namesake, begins his prophecy similarly, "Hearken, O people, every one of you." Micah designedly uses the same preface, implying that his ministrations are a continuation of his predecessor's of the same name. Both probably had before their mind Moses' similar attestation of heaven and earth in a like case (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.28">De 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">32:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God be witness against you--</hi>namely, that none of you can say, when the time of your punishment shall come, that you were not forewarned. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12718"/><div sID="gen23529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12718"/>4. Imagery from earthquakes and volcanic agency, to describe the terrors which attend Jehovah's coming in judgment (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.5.5">Jud 5:5</reference>). Neither men of high degree, as the mountains, nor men of low degree, as the valleys, can secure themselves or their land from the judgments of God.<div eID="gen23529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as wax--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.97.5">Psa 97:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.3">Is 64:1-3</reference>). The third clause, "as wax," &c., answers to the first in the parallelism, "the mountains shall be molten"; the fourth, "as the waters," &c., to the second, "the valleys shall be cleft." As wax melts by fire, so the mountains before God, at His approach; and as waters poured down a steep cannot stand but are diffused abroad, so the valleys shall be cleft before Jehovah. <div eID="gen23530" type="x-p"/>

Samaria's punishment is mentioned first, as it was to fall before Jerusalem.<div eID="gen23534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as an heap of the field--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>). Samaria was destroyed by Shalmaneser. <div eID="gen23538" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12721"/><div sID="gen23539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12721"/><hi type="bold">7. all the hires--</hi>the wealth which Israel boasted of receiving from her idols as the "rewards" or "hire" for worshipping them (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.5">Ho 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">idols ... will I ... desolate--</hi>that is, give them up to the foe to strip off the silver and gold with which they are overlaid.<div eID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot--</hi>Israel gathered (made for herself) her idols from the gold and silver received from false gods, as she thought, the "hire" of her worshipping them; and they shall again become what they had been before, the hire of spiritual harlotry, that is, the prosperity of the foe, who also being worshippers of idols will ascribe the acquisition to their idols [Maurer]. Grotius explains it, The offerings sent to Israel's temple by the Assyrians, whose idolatry Israel adopted, shall go back to the Assyrians, her teachers in idolatry, as the hire or fee for having taught it. The image of a harlot's hire for the supposed temporal reward of spiritual fornication, is more common in Scripture (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Ho 9:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23541" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: INTRODUCTION Micah was a native of Moresheth, not the same as Mareshah in Mi 1:15 , but the town called Moresheth-gath ( Mi 1:14 ), which lay near Eleutheropolis, west of Jerusalem, on the border of the Philistine country; so called to distinguish it from Moresheth of Judah. His full name is Micaiah (not the Micaiah mentioned 1Ki 22:8 , the son of Imlah), signifying, Who is like Jehovah? The time of his prophesying is stated in the introduction to be in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, that is, between 757 and 699 B.C. Jeremiah ( Jr 26:18 ) quotes Mi 3:12 , as delivered in the reign of Hezekiah. He was thus a contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea. The idolatries practised in the reign of Ahaz accord with Micah's denunciations of such gross evils, and confirm the truth of the time assigned Mi 1:1 . His prophecies are partly against Israel (Samaria), partly against Judah. As Samaria, Israel's metropolis, was taken first, and Jerusalem, the capital of Judah subsequently, in the introductory heading, Mi 1:1 , Samaria is put first, then Jerusalem. He prophesies the capture of both; the Jews' captivity and restoration; and the coming and reign of Messiah. His style is full, round, and perspicuous; his diction pure, and his parallelisms regular. His description of Jehovah ( Mi 7:18 , 19 ) is not surpassed by any elsewhere in Scripture. The similarity between Isaiah and Micah in some passages (compare Mi 4:1-3 , with Is 2:2-4 ) is to be accounted for by their being contemporaries, acquainted with each other's inspired writings, and having the same subjects for their theme. Hengstenberg maintains that the passage in Micah is the original. Isaiah was somewhat the older, being a prophet in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham's predecessor, whereas Micah began his prophecies under Jotham. The book consists of two parts: (1) the first through fifth chapters; (2) the sixth and seventh chapters, a dialogue or contestation between Jehovah and His people, in which He reproaches them with their unnatural and ungrateful conduct, and threatens judgment for their corruptions, but consoles them with the promise of restoration from captivity. Micah stands sixth of the minor prophets in the Hebrew canon, but third in the Septuagint.

Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jr 26:18</reference>) quotes <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>, as delivered in the reign of Hezekiah. He was thus a contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea. The idolatries practised in the reign of Ahaz accord with Micah's denunciations of such gross evils, and confirm the truth of the time assigned <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>. His prophecies are partly against Israel (Samaria), partly against Judah. As Samaria, Israel's metropolis, was taken first, and Jerusalem, the capital of Judah subsequently, in the introductory heading, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.1">Mi 1:1</reference>, Samaria is put first, then Jerusalem. He prophesies the capture of both; the Jews' captivity and restoration; and the coming and reign of Messiah. His style is full, round, and perspicuous; his diction pure, and his parallelisms regular. His description of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">19</reference>) is not surpassed by any elsewhere in Scripture. The similarity between Isaiah and Micah in some passages (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.3">Mi 4:1-3</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>) is to be accounted for by their being contemporaries, acquainted with each other's inspired writings, and having the same subjects for their theme. Hengstenberg maintains that the passage in Micah is the original. Isaiah was somewhat the older, being a prophet in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham's predecessor, whereas Micah began his prophecies under Jotham.<div eID="gen23522" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23521" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> The book consists of two parts: (1) the first through fifth chapters; (2) the sixth and seventh chapters, a dialogue or contestation between Jehovah and His people, in which He reproaches them with their unnatural and ungrateful conduct, and threatens judgment for their corruptions, but consoles them with the promise of restoration from captivity.<div eID="gen23523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23524" type="x-p"/> Micah stands sixth of the minor prophets in the Hebrew canon, but third in the Septuagint.<div eID="gen23524" type="x-p"/>
